analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans personally import cheaper prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan support in July 2024, was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the federal government, within 180 days, to set up rules letting individuals buy prescription drugs from pharmacies in Canada that meet safety and licensing standards set by the Health and Human Services Secretary. People could import up to a 90-day supply for personal use, with a valid US prescription, and the FDA would publish a list of approved Canadian pharmacies. Certain higher-risk drugs — controlled substances, biologics, injectables, and refrigerated drugs — would be excluded.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay US prices for prescription drugs, especially people on fixed incomes or without generous insurance, who could buy the same medications from vetted Canadian pharmacies where prices are often much lower because Canada regulates drug prices.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to issue regulations within 180 days permitting individuals to safely import qualifying prescription drugs from Canada [S2].

Limits imports to a 90-day personal-use supply, purchased from a Canadian pharmacy certified as licensed and meeting safety criteria, using a valid US prescription, and containing the same active ingredients, dosage form, and strength as an FDA-approved drug [S2].
Mandates that the FDA publish a public list of approved Canadian pharmacies, including their website addresses, so consumers know which sellers are vetted [S2].

Certification criteria require pharmacies to have operated for at least five years, follow Canadian provincial pharmacy standards, run quality-assurance and product-testing programs through Secretary-approved laboratories, and refrain from reselling drugs from non-Canadian online pharmacies [S2].

Excludes higher-risk products from importation — controlled substances, biological products, infused and intravenous drugs, biotechnology-derived products, refrigerated drugs, and photoreactive drugs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose US sales would face competition from lower Canadian prices on the same drugs; the bill also imposes implementation costs on HHS and the FDA for certifying and monitoring pharmacies.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on the Secretary to certify pharmacies and approve laboratories for testing, so safety would depend on regulatory implementation; the restrictions on biologic and refrigerated drugs also mean many expensive modern medicines, including most cancer biologics, would not be importable at all [S2].

Personal importation addresses only individual purchases and would not change prices paid through employer insurance, Medicare, or pharmacy benefit channels, so the savings reach mainly those who pay out of pocket and can navigate online ordering [S2].

Critics of drug importation generally argue that FDA oversight of foreign supply chains cannot fully guarantee drug authenticity and safety; the bill mitigates this with certification and testing requirements but leaves judgment about sufficiency to the Secretary [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people paying steep out-of-pocket drug costs, the bill offered a direct path to lower prices with meaningful guardrails: only vetted pharmacies, 90-day personal-use limits, same-drug equivalence requirements, and exclusions of the riskiest product categories. The main costs fall on brand-name drug makers, whose US pricing power would erode at the margin. The design is narrower than a systemwide importation program — it does nothing for drugs bought through insurance pipelines and excludes biologics — but within its scope it is a consumer benefit with modest safety risk, which opponents have historically cited to keep similar measures from becoming law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and the Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on July 31, 2024, joined by seven other senators, including Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley, giving it bipartisan sponsorship [S1] [S2].

The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced; the action history shows no further action, hearing, markup, or vote [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without reaching the Senate floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off, since Canadian price competition for individual purchasers never arrived; consumers paying high US drug prices remain where they were.

against.what_they_did: Has long lobbied against Canadian drug importation on safety grounds; the industry's opposition is not documented in this bill's record, so this reflects general public reporting.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan: 6 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican (Sen. Grassley) among the 8 original sponsors [S2] [S3].

industries.note: The bill would let individuals buy the same drugs from Canada, where government-regulated prices are typically far lower, undercutting US list prices for personal-use purchases. It excludes biologics, the priciest modern drugs, limiting the revenue impact but not the precedent.

Certified Canadian pharmacies would gain a legal channel to sell to US customers, with FDA publishing their websites. Only pharmacies with at least five years of operation and quality-assurance programs qualify, favoring established Canadian sellers.

industries.industry: US pharmacy benefit managers and retail pharmacies
industries.note: Personal importation bypasses the US pharmacy and PBM chain for direct purchasers, though the 90-day personal-use limit and exclusion of insured-channel drugs keep the effect modest.
